title: The Questions Engaged Couples Are Afraid to Ask
paragraphs:
The Questions Engaged Couples Are Afraid to Ask
The Conversation That Could Save Your Marriage Before You Ever Say “I Do”
Some couples spend thousands of dollars preparing for one unforgettable wedding day.
Very few spend enough time preparing for fifty unforgettable years.
Not because they don't love each other.
But because love often hides behind excitement, and excitement can silence the questions that desperately need to be asked.
Some questions feel like they might ruin everything.
Meanwhile, hidden fears quietly grow roots beneath the surface.
The Bible never presents marriage as merely a romantic celebration.

The Hebrew word often associated with covenant is בְּרִית (Berit)—a binding agreement established with solemn commitment, not temporary emotion. Throughout Scripture, covenant is stronger than feelings. Feelings rise and fall. Covenant remains.
That is why marriage reflects something infinitely greater than two people falling in love.

"For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
The Greek word translated "joined" is προσκολληθήσεται (proskollēthēsetai), carrying the idea of being glued together, permanently attached, inseparable.
Marriage was never designed to be two people trying each other out.
It is two lives becoming one.
Which is exactly why honest questions matter.
Not because you're looking for reasons to leave.
Because you're looking for reasons to stay.
The first question many couples fear asking is this:
Dating is often our edited version.
Marriage eventually reveals the unedited version.
How does your future spouse respond to failure?
How do they respond when prayers seem unanswered?
How do they react when life becomes unfair?
"Count it all joy... when you meet trials..."
Another question couples quietly avoid is this:
Not because someone married the wrong person.
Because two sinners cannot create a sinless relationship.
The Greek word Jesus repeatedly uses for forgiveness is ἀφίημι (aphiēmi).
It literally carries the meaning of releasing, sending away, letting go.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
It is refusing to keep demanding payment after Christ has already paid the greatest debt.
If someone cannot forgive small offenses before marriage...
Many people enter marriage believing love will heal childhood trauma.
But your spouse was never meant to replace Jesus.
"He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds."
Another question almost nobody wants to ask:
Jesus spoke about money more than many people realize.
Not because God wants our wallets.
Because our treasure reveals our hearts.
"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
The Greek word καρδία (kardia) means heart—not merely emotion—but the center of one's will, identity, desires, and inner life.
Instead, it commands us not to let anger rule us.
The Greek word ὀργή (orgē) often describes settled wrath—anger that refuses to leave.
"What role does Jesus actually have in your life?"
Not your Christian social media posts.
"Who do you say that I am?"
Every engaged couple should answer that individually.
Because no marriage can rise above its deepest foundation.
"Everyone who hears these words of Mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock."
The Greek word πέτρα (petra) means solid bedrock.
Every healthy marriage requires radical honesty before lifelong intimacy.
"Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed."
Perhaps the hardest question of all.
"If God changed our plans tomorrow, would we still choose Him first?"
"Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."
The Greek word αὐτός (autos) emphasizes that it is the very same Jesus—unchanging in His character and faithfulness.
Some people reading this are engaged.
Others have been married for decades.
Some wish someone had asked them these questions years ago.
But here's the breathtaking hope of the Gospel.
Jesus has always specialized in rewriting broken stories.
The woman caught in adultery expected public shame.
Peter expected permanent failure after denying Christ.
The thief on the cross expected judgment.
The Gospel has always been a story of scandal transformed by grace.
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
The Greek word συνίστησιν (synistēsin) means to demonstrate, prove, or establish beyond question.
God did not merely say He loves us.
Perhaps the greatest question every engaged couple must answer is not whether they love each other enough.
It is whether both are daily surrendering to the One who first loved them.
Marriage without Christ may survive for a season.
Marriage centered on Christ can glorify God through every season.
If this article challenged you, don't keep it to yourself. Someone in your circle may need this conversation more than you realize.
Sometimes God uses one shared article to begin a conversation that changes an entire family legacy.
The questions worth asking before marriage are often the ones we need to revisit after the wedding, especially when life becomes difficult.
Because someday, your wedding photos will become old memories.
But a marriage built on Christ will keep telling His story long after the flowers have faded.
